title: Jekyll and Hyde: context and the extract question
specPoints: Paper 1 Section B: the 19th-century novel, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
AO3: the relationships between the text and its contexts

why.matters: Six of the thirty marks on the novel are for context, and the June 2024 mark scheme listed four kinds: good and evil, hidden aspects of character, science and the unknown, and the Gothic. Each of them explains something Stevenson chose: a face nobody can describe, a respectable man who hides, a drug that crosses a line, a city of fog. Learning the few facts that do that work, tied to lines, turns a list of history into an argument about the book.

examples.title: A real double life
examples.body: Deacon Brodie, respected councillor by day and burglar by night, was a story Edinburgh still told when Stevenson was a boy. News stories of respected people with secret lives still carry the same shock, and the same question the novel asks: which one was the real person?

examples.title: The monster made by science
examples.body: From Frankenstein to modern films about experiments that go wrong, the scientist who creates what he cannot control is a lasting story. Stevenson's version is unusual in that the creature is the scientist himself.

steps.title: Stevenson and a double life
steps.body:
Robert Louis Stevenson was born in Edinburgh in 1850 into a respectable, strictly religious family of engineers. *Jekyll and Hyde* appeared in 1886; Stevenson said the idea came to him in a dream.

**Edinburgh's double life.** Edinburgh remembered Deacon William Brodie, a respected cabinet-maker and town councillor by day and a burglar by night, hanged in 1788. Stevenson had written a play about him with W. E. Henley. The city itself had two faces: the elegant New Town and the crowded Old Town below it.

**Why it matters for AO3.** Six of the thirty marks are for context. On this novel the useful contexts are the ones that explain its fear: respectability, science, the Gothic, and the idea of a hidden self.

steps.title: Respectability: the Victorian gentleman
steps.body:
The men of the novel are professionals: a lawyer, doctors, a Member of Parliament. Their standing depended on reputation, and reputation depended on what was not said.

**What respectability forbade.** Jekyll describes himself hiding pleasures that his standing would not allow: “I concealed my pleasures”. He never names them. The novel's silence is the period's.

**The gentleman's code.** Enfield will not ask, “the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask”; Utterson will not judge, “I incline to Cain’s heresy”. Discretion was a virtue, and the novel shows it becoming a cover.

**How to use it.** Tie it to a line: *Because a gentleman's standing rested on his reputation, Jekyll's need to plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability is what makes Hyde necessary.*

check.solution: Respectable men did not name such things in print. By leaving them unnamed, Stevenson keeps faith with the code he is exposing, and the reader supplies what the gentleman will not say.

steps.title: Science, Darwin and the beast within
steps.body:
**Evolution.** Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* (1859) and *The Descent of Man* (1871) placed human beings among the animals. Stevenson's readers would hear that in Hyde: “Something troglodytic, shall we say?”, “with ape-like fury”.

**Degeneration and the criminal face.** In 1876 the Italian criminologist Cesare Lombroso argued that criminals were throwbacks to a primitive type who could be recognised by their features. Everyone who sees Hyde senses something wrong in his face, and cannot say what.

**Science that trespasses.** Jekyll's experiment goes where Victorian religion said science should not: into the soul. Lanyon's material science calls it “unscientific balderdash”; the proof kills him.

The June 2024 indicative content included ideas about fear of the unknown and scientific discovery and exploration.

check.prompt: How does Darwin's work help explain the fear of Hyde for an 1886 reader?
check.solution: Evolution suggested that the civilised man had come from something wilder. Hyde, ape-like and troglodytic, is that wildness returned, inside a respectable doctor.

markScheme.description: If man descended from animals, the primitive might still be inside the gentleman, and Hyde's ape-like fury makes that fear visible

It does not help

Because Darwin wrote a review of the novel saying that Hyde was a scientifically accurate description of a human ancestor, which made readers believe that Hyde was a real creature

steps.title: The Gothic: doubles, darkness, the city
steps.body:
The novel belongs to the Gothic tradition: fiction of fear, secrets and the supernatural, with dark settings and the threat of something monstrous. The June 2024 indicative content included ideas about aspects of Gothic literature creating fear and danger.

**The double.** Gothic fiction often gives a character a dark twin. Stevenson makes the twin the same man: “these polar twins should be continuously struggling”.

**The city instead of the castle.** Earlier Gothic novels used castles and ruins. Stevenson's Gothic is modern London at night: fog, lamps, a “like a district of some city in a nightmare”.

**Science as the new supernatural.** Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein* (1818) had already made a scientist the maker of a monster. Jekyll's drug is Gothic magic in a laboratory.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on Gothic features in the novel: the double, darkness, the monster, and forbidden knowledge

check.prompt: How does Stevenson update the Gothic for 1886?
check.solution: Fog, lamps and a respectable street replace the ruined abbey; a chemist's drug replaces the curse. The fear is closer to home because the setting is the reader's own city.

markScheme.description: He moves the terror from castles to modern London and makes science do what magic did

options: He sets the novel in a medieval castle in Scotland with ghosts and a haunted tower, and Hyde is the ghost of Jekyll's grandfather who returns every night to take revenge on the family
He makes it a comedy
He removes all darkness from the story
He moves the terror from castles to modern London and makes science do what magic did

steps.title: The June 2024 extract, read with the question
steps.body:
The paper said: *In this extract, Utterson is alone thinking about Mr Hyde.* Then it printed this passage from Chapter 2, as AQA's edition gives it.

> That was the amount of information that the lawyer carried back with him to the great, dark bed on which he tossed to and fro, until the small hours of the morning began to grow large. It was a night of little ease to his toiling mind, toiling in mere darkness and besieged by questions.
>
> Six o'clock struck on the bells of the church that was so conveniently near to Mr. Utterson's dwelling, and still he was digging at the problem. Hitherto it had touched him on the intellectual side alone; but now his imagination also was engaged, or rather enslaved; and as he lay and tossed in the gross darkness of the night and the curtained room, Mr. Enfield's tale went by before his mind in a scroll of lighted pictures. He would be aware of the great field of lamps of a nocturnal city; then of the figure of a man walking swiftly; then of a child running from the doctor's; and then these met, and that human Juggernaut trod the child down and passed on regardless of her screams. Or else he would see a room in a rich house, where his friend lay asleep, dreaming and smiling at his dreams; and then the door of that room would be opened, the curtains of the bed plucked apart, the sleeper recalled, and lo! there would stand by his side a figure to whom power was given, and even at that dead hour he must rise and do its bidding. The figure in these two phases haunted the lawyer all night; and if at any time he dozed over, it was but to see it glide more stealthily through sleeping houses, or move the more swiftly and still the more swiftly, even to dizziness, through wider labyrinths of lamplighted city, and at every street corner crush a child and leave her screaming. And still the figure had no face by which he might know it; even in his dreams, it had no face, or one that baffled him and melted before his eyes; and thus it was that there sprang up and grew apace in the lawyer's mind a singularly strong, almost an inordinate, curiosity to behold the features of the real Mr. Hyde. If he could but once set eyes on him, he thought the mystery would lighten and perhaps roll altogether away, as was the habit of mysterious things when well examined. He might see a reason for his friend's strange preference or bondage (call it which you please) and even for the startling clauses of the will. And at least it would be a face worth seeing: the face of a man who was without bowels of mercy: a face which had but to show itself to raise up, in the mind of the unimpressionable Enfield, a spirit of enduring hatred.
>
> From that time forward, Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the by-street of shops. In the morning before office hours, at noon when business was plenty and time scarce, at night under the face of the fogged city moon, by all lights and at all hours of solitude or concourse, the lawyer was to be found on his chosen post.

**The question.** Starting with this extract, explore how Stevenson creates an atmosphere of fear and danger in the novel. Write about how he does it in this extract, and in the novel as a whole. 30 marks.

steps.title: Methods in the extract, each with an effect
steps.body:
**Night and darkness.** The great dark bed, the small hours, “toiling in mere darkness and besieged by questions”: the military verb *besieged* makes the questions an enemy.

**A film in the mind.** “a scroll of lighted pictures”: the story replays like pictures, and the reader watches with him.

**Repetition and acceleration.** The figure moves “that human Juggernaut trod the child down” and then swifter, still more swiftly, “through wider labyrinths of lamplighted city”, “at every street corner crush a child and leave her screaming”: the sentences speed up as the nightmare does.

**Power and bondage.** In the second picture, by Jekyll's bed, stands “a figure to whom power was given”, and even at that dead hour he must rise and do its bidding. Utterson imagines blackmail; the reader of Chapter 10 knows it was worse.

**Obsession.** “Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the by-street of shops”, “under the face of the fogged city moon”: the lawyer becomes a ghost at the door.

steps.title: Write the opening and one paragraph
steps.body:
Using the plan, write:

1. An opening of two sentences: an idea about how Stevenson creates fear and danger across the novel.
2. One paragraph on the extract: two methods, each with a line and an effect.

Then check it against the Level 6 descriptor: a conceptualised response, judicious references, analysis of methods with subject terminology used judiciously, and context shown by specific links.

**No AO4 on this question.** The four marks for accuracy on Paper 1 go to the Shakespeare question only, but accuracy still helps the examiner follow the argument.

steps.title: Context that explains a choice
steps.body:
The Level 6 descriptor for AO3 asks for exploration of ideas, perspectives or contextual factors shown by specific, detailed links between context, text and task.

**Tie it.** *Because a gentleman's standing depended on his reputation* is context; *Jekyll concealed his pleasures* is the line. Join them.

**Explain a choice.** Why is Hyde described by effect and not by feature? Because a reader who had read of Lombroso's criminal faces, or of Darwin's apes, could supply the face.

**Serve the task.** On fear and danger, the Gothic and Darwin serve; on Utterson's character, respectability serves.

**One sentence.** Inside the argument, never before it.

steps.title: Context and the extract question in one page
steps.body:
Stevenson's Edinburgh, a gentleman's reputation, Darwin's animal in man, and the Gothic moved to London.

- **Stevenson:** born Edinburgh 1850; Deacon Brodie; the novel from a dream; 1886.
- **Respectability:** reputation as a gentleman's capital; pleasures never named; discretion as a cover.
- **Science:** Darwin 1859 and 1871; Lombroso's criminal face; science against religion.
- **The Gothic:** the double, darkness, the monster, forbidden knowledge; the city for the castle.
- **June 2024:** Chapter 2, Utterson's sleepless night; night, labyrinth, facelessness, the Juggernaut echo.
- **The question:** 30 marks, no AO4; start in the extract, move out, tie context to a line.

questions.prompt: Starting with the June 2024 extract, explore how Stevenson creates an atmosphere of fear and danger. Write the opening idea and a paragraph on the extract.
questions.solution: Stevenson creates fear by withholding what the reader most wants to see, and the city at night gives the unseen room to grow. In this extract a respectable lawyer cannot sleep: his mind is “toiling in mere darkness and besieged by questions”, and the military verb makes the questions an army around him. His imagination is “his imagination also was engaged, or rather enslaved”, so that the man of reason has lost control of his own thoughts. The story he has heard replays as “a scroll of lighted pictures”, and then accelerates: the figure moves more swiftly “through wider labyrinths of lamplighted city”, and the repetition, “at every street corner crush a child and leave her screaming”, turns one crime into an endless one. Most frightening of all, “even in his dreams, it had no face, or one that baffled him and melted before his eyes”. In the Gothic tradition, fear lives in what is hidden, and Stevenson makes Hyde the purest case: not a monster described but a blank that Utterson's mind cannot fill. The respectable man who wants to see the face is also the man who will spend the novel not asking the question that would show it.

His imagination is “his imagination also was engaged, or rather enslaved”, so that the man of reason has lost control of his own thoughts. Most frightening of all, “even in his dreams, it had no face, or one that baffled him and melted before his eyes”. In the Gothic tradition, fear lives in what is hidden, and Stevenson makes Hyde the purest case: not a monster described but a blank that Utterson's mind cannot fill. The respectable man who wants to see the face is also the man who will spend the novel not asking the question that would show it.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph moving from the June 2024 extract to fear and danger elsewhere in the novel.
questions.solution: The nightmare in Chapter 2 is fed by Chapter 1: “that human Juggernaut trod the child down and passed on regardless of her screams” echoes Enfield's own word, so that a story told on a Sunday walk becomes a haunting. The fear then leaves Utterson's mind and enters the world. In Chapter 4 a maid watches Hyde attack an old man “with ape-like fury”, and “the bones were audibly shattered”; the city is covered by fog like “A great chocolate-coloured pall lowered over heaven”, and Soho is “like a district of some city in a nightmare”, as if Utterson's dream had become the street. On the last night the danger is inside a locked room: “A dismal screech, as of mere animal terror”. And the final document moves fear inside the self: Jekyll writes “I felt younger, lighter, happier in body”, and then that he was “I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self”. The novel's fear travels from a faceless figure in a dream to a man who can no longer be sure which face is his.

questions.prompt: A student begins with a paragraph on Victorian London's population, industry and fog. What is the better approach?
questions.solution: The top level asks for context shown by specific, detailed links between context, text and task. A paragraph of background with no line earns little; a sentence that explains a choice earns more.

markScheme.description: Put context in single sentences tied to lines, chosen for the task, inside the argument

options: The student is right to begin with a full paragraph of context, because the examiner needs to see the background first before any analysis of the extract can be given any marks at all
Leave context out entirely
Put context in single sentences tied to lines, chosen for the task, inside the argument
Write the context at the end only

questions.prompt: How should an answer use the fact that there are no AO4 marks on the Jekyll and Hyde question?
questions.solution: AO4 marks are on the Shakespeare question. On the novel, all thirty marks are for AO1, AO2 and AO3, but a clear argument is still how those marks are earned.

markScheme.description: Spend the time on analysis and the whole-text move, while writing clearly enough to be followed

options: Answer the Macbeth question twice
Write in note form and bullet points to save time, because spelling, punctuation and sentence structure are not assessed at all on this question and so the examiner will not read them
Write as little as possible
Spend the time on analysis and the whole-text move, while writing clearly enough to be followed

examTechnique.body:
**Thirty marks, no AO4.** AO1 12, AO2 12, AO3 6.

**Start in the extract.** Name the methods: night, verbs, repetition, the labyrinth, the missing face.

**Move out on the same focus.** Pair the extract with Chapter 1, 4, 8 or 10.

**Context in a sentence, tied to a line.** The Gothic and the faceless figure; respectability and Jekyll's concealment; Darwin and ape-like.
examinerErrors: A paragraph of Victorian history before the answer.
Quoting loosely from memory: learn the exact words.
Treating the novel as a simple story of good and evil.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer opens with an idea about fear or the chosen focus across the novel, analyses the extract's methods closely, moves out to two or three other moments with exact quotations, and ties context to lines: the Gothic to the faceless figure, respectability to Jekyll's concealment, Darwin to the ape-like fury. It reads the extract twice, as Utterson and as a reader who knows the ending.
